# Results — Study 533 (Analyst-Dispersion / Diether-Malloy-Scherbina puzzle)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — Diether,
Malloy & Scherbina (2002): **stocks with high dispersion in analysts' earnings forecasts earn
LOWER returns** (a puzzle versus the risk intuition that disagreement should demand a higher
premium). We build the dispersion proxy from yfinance's per-name analyst EPS-estimate spread,
`dispersion = (high − low) / |mean|` on the current-fiscal-year (`0y`) consensus, sort a fixed
40-name large-cap basket into dispersion terciles, and test the **low-minus-high** long-short.
Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.
As-of **2026-06-26**.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance `Ticker.earnings_estimate` (0y EPS low/mean/high) + daily adjusted closes — 40 long-listed US large-caps (public, no key) |
| Dispersion snapshot | 40 names, fingerprint `272030376053` (pulled 2026-06-26) |
| Price tape | 2015-01-02 → 2026-06-26 (2,887 days × 40 tickers), fingerprint `8691afedbd40` |
| Dispersion measure | `(high − low) / |mean|` of the current-fiscal-year consensus EPS estimate — the free DMS proxy |
| Sort / return / costs | tercile sort; **long low-dispersion, short high-dispersion**; trailing **1 / 3 / 6 / 12-month** return; **10 bps** one-way × 4 legs + **100 bps/yr** borrow on the short leg |

> **The central data limitation (named on the Signal axis).** yfinance exposes only the
> **current** analyst-estimate snapshot — there is **no historical dispersion panel**. So we
> cannot build the month-by-month *forward* sort the academic study uses; the dispersion column
> is a single cross-section stamped on the pull date, and the only honest thing to do with it is
> sort it against the **trailing** return realised into that date. That is a *contemporaneous
> association*, not a deployable forward strategy, and it rests on **one cross-section of 40
> survivor names**. Every number below carries that caveat. A true replication needs a vendor
> dispersion history (I/B/E/S) — out of reach for this free-data desk.

> **Survivorship (also named).** The basket is 40 names *still trading* in 2026. The surviving
> high-dispersion names (NVDA, TSLA, ORCL, META, AMZN) are exactly the multi-baggers; their
> failed high-dispersion peers are gone from the tape. This biases the high-dispersion (short)
> leg's realised return strongly *upward* — i.e. *against* the DMS prediction — at the long
> horizons. We read the result with that mechanism front of mind.

## The signal — low-minus-high dispersion long-short (DMS direction: low should win)

Long the low-dispersion tercile, short the high-dispersion tercile; the *t* is a one-sample *t*
of the pooled per-name long-short sample against 0; the placebo *p* is the two-sided share of
20,000 **dispersion-label shuffles** whose random low-minus-high spread is at least as large in
magnitude as the observed one. Spearman is the rank correlation of dispersion vs the return
(DMS predicts **negative**).

| trailing H | n | low-disp mean | high-disp mean | low−high | win-rate | one-sample *t* | placebo *p* | Spearman ρ |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **1-mo** | 40 | +3.37% | −7.09% | **+10.46%** | 74% | **+3.21** | **0.003** | **−0.435** |
| 3-mo | 40 | +12.52% | +20.19% | −7.67% | 59% | −0.39 | 0.633 | −0.120 |
| 6-mo | 40 | +8.06% | +26.32% | −18.26% | 48% | −0.82 | 0.341 | −0.108 |
| 12-mo | 40 | +16.35% | +56.11% | −39.76% | 41% | −0.99 | 0.237 | +0.105 |

Read it carefully. There is **exactly one** horizon — the trailing **1-month** — where the DMS
direction shows up, and it shows up *loudly*: low-dispersion names beat high-dispersion names by
**+10.46%** at **t = 3.21** (placebo *p* = 0.003, Spearman −0.435). But this is a **single
cross-section on a single date**: the +3.21 is the snapshot catching a recent month in which the
crowded high-dispersion names (TSLA, ORCL, BA) sold off together — it is one window, not a
replicated effect, and it **cannot be averaged over independent draws** the way the desk's bar
requires. At **every longer horizon the sign flips hard**: over the trailing year high-dispersion
names *out-earned* low-dispersion by **39.8 percentage points** (*t* = −0.99). The longer the
window, the more the survivorship winners dominate.

## Monotonicity — the 12-month picture runs the WRONG way for DMS

12-month trailing return by dispersion tercile (low → high):

| Tercile | low-disp (T1) | mid (T2) | high-disp (T3) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 12-mo return | **+16.35%** | +35.89% | **+56.11%** |

Cleanly **monotone increasing** in dispersion — the *opposite* of the DMS prediction. On this
survivor basket, more disagreement went with *higher* realised returns, exactly the
survivorship shadow: the high-dispersion names that survived to 2026 are the ones whose bet paid
off.

## Costs — moot, because there is no forward trade

For completeness we charge the implied trade (10 bps one-way × 4 legs + 100 bps/yr borrow on the
short leg over the horizon):

| trailing H | gross low−high | net of costs |
|---|--:|--:|
| 1-mo | +10.46% | **+9.98%** |
| 3-mo | −7.67% | −8.32% |
| 6-mo | −18.26% | −19.16% |
| 12-mo | −39.76% | −41.16% |

Costs barely move the 1-month number (+9.98% net) — but this is **not a tradable result**: the
return is *trailing* (already realised into the snapshot), so "net" here is a bookkeeping
exercise, not a P&L you could have captured. You cannot trade a contemporaneous association.

## Robustness — the 12-month reversal is not a bucket-count artefact

| bucket count | low−high (12-mo) | *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2 (halves) | −30.15% | −1.08 | 0.288 |
| **3 (terciles)** | **−39.76%** | **−0.99** | **0.237** |
| 5 (quintiles) | −53.62% | −0.85 | 0.229 |

The wrong-sign, insignificant 12-month result is stable across bucket counts; tighter buckets
only widen the (wrong-direction) spread. The lone right-sign 1-month spike is the outlier, not
the rule.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic multi-period panel where dispersion **does** drag returns down by a planted
`dms_edge` (DMS sign). Averaged over 25 seeds (a seed-robust power check, *never* cited for the
real stamp):

| planted DMS edge | avg low−high spread | avg one-sample *t* | frac. of seeds with *t* > 2 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (null) | −0.47% | **+0.167** | 0% |
| **0.70** (large planted) | +65.30% | **+2.629** | **100%** |

With **no** planted edge the sort sits at *t* ≈ 0.17 (it does not manufacture significance from
noise); a large planted DMS drag lights up at *t* ≈ 2.63 on **every** seed. The cross-sectional
sort engine is unbiased and adequately powered — so the real-tape result is a genuine reading of
the (survivor-biased, single-snapshot) tape, not a construction artefact.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The DMS direction (low dispersion out-earns high) appears at **exactly one**
  horizon — trailing 1-month, **+10.46% at t = 3.21, placebo p = 0.003, Spearman −0.435** — but
  this is a **single cross-section on a single date**, the snapshot catching one month's crowded
  high-dispersion selloff. It cannot be averaged over independent draws, and it is **contradicted
  at every longer horizon** (3 / 6 / 12-month all wrong-sign, the 12-month tercile sort cleanly
  *monotone the wrong way*). A lone window's *t* > 3 on one cross-section is exactly the case the
  desk grades **WEAK, not REAL** — there is literature support (DMS 2002 is a real, replicated
  academic effect) but no robust, design-stable real-tape confirmation here.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is **no forward trade** to deploy: yfinance gives only a current
  dispersion snapshot, so the sort is against *trailing* returns — a contemporaneous association,
  not a strategy. The "net +9.98%" at 1-month is bookkeeping on already-realised returns, not P&L.
  On a 40-name survivor basket with no dispersion history, this cannot be made investable with the
  available free data.
- **"Does high dispersion really earn LESS?" — MIXED.** The honest answer on this tape is
  *direction-dependent and horizon-dependent*: yes at 1 month (the freshest snapshot), no — in
  fact strongly reversed — at 3–12 months, where the surviving high-dispersion winners dominate.
  The academic puzzle is real in the literature, but on a free, single-snapshot, survivor-tilted
  cross-section it does not cleanly replicate.
